governanceNotes: D1 batch 51 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - labyrinthitis to hearing-loss (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true; mechanismCategory INFECTIOUS_SPREAD. The proposition rests on the Maranhao 2016 retrospective cohort drawn from 26 years of admissions for middle-ear-infection-associated labyrinthitis, which identified 14 patients (mean age 40 years; cholesteatomatous chronic otitis media in six, acute suppurative otitis media in six, chronic otitis media without cholesteatoma in two) with 24 concomitant complications (labyrinthine fistula in six, meningitis in five, facial paralysis in five, mastoiditis in five, cerebellar abscess in two, temporal abscess in one, and one death), and in which eight patients (57%) became deaf and six (43%) acquired mixed hearing loss, leading the authors to conclude that the hearing sequela of labyrinthitis was significant; it rests also on the Taxak and Ram 2020 case report and literature review of labyrinthitis and labyrinthitis ossificans, which describes inflammatory disruption of sensory transmission from ear to brain and defines labyrinthitis ossificans as pathological ossification of the membranous labyrinthine spaces in response to an inner-ear insult involving the membranous labyrinth or the endosteum of the otic capsule, presenting with progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss is thus documented as the principal residual sequela of labyrinthitis at cohort and review level.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) source pathway - the cohort's labyrinthitis arose from middle-ear infection (cholesteatomatous and suppurative otitis media), so the edge records the suppurative route rather than all causes of inner-ear inflammation and does not extend to viral or autoimmune labyrinthitis; (ii) severity selection - the cohort is an inpatient, referral, complication-rich series with 24 concomitant complications, so the 57% deafness figure reflects severe disease and does not describe the common mild labyrinthitis episode; (iii) small sample - fourteen patients over 26 years, so no population-level incidence can be inferred; (iv) outcome heterogeneity - six patients (43%) had mixed rather than purely sensorineural loss, reflecting the coexisting middle-ear disease, so the audiometric character must be documented in the individual case; (v) competing causes - sudden sensorineural hearing loss has multiple independent causes (vascular, viral, autoimmune, and retrocochlear disease, including vestibular schwannoma) that must be excluded before attributing loss to labyrinthitis.

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) no labyrinthitis-to-vestibular-disorder edge - the harvested proposition remains FINAL-CLOSED under FINAL-CLOSE-PROPOSITION-MISMATCH and is not reasserted (prior-closure guard); (ii) no dizziness, vertigo, or benign-paroxysmal-positional-vertigo edge - vestibular symptoms are constitutive of the acute labyrinthitis presentation and the located secondary-BPPV literature is head-trauma, Meniere, vestibular-neuritis, and sensorineural-hearing-loss anchored rather than labyrinthitis-specific (constitutive and zero-record guards); (iii) no tinnitus edge - no condition-specific labyrinthitis tinnitus quantification was located (zero-record guard); (iv) no meningitis, facial-paralysis, or mastoiditis edge - those were concomitant complications recorded alongside labyrinthitis in a mixed middle-ear-disease cohort rather than labyrinthitis-specific downstream diagnoses, and the meningitis window on hearing-loss is authored from its own primary (wrong-direction attribution and duplicate-scope guards); (v) no visual-impairment or cognitive-disorder edge (zero-record guard); (vi) duplicate-scope note: the hearing-loss identity's existing four windows are not pre-empted by this suppurative inner-ear window.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Maranhao 2016 retrospective cohort of 26 years of admissions for middle-ear-infection-associated labyrinthitis identified 14 patients (mean age 40 years) with 24 concomitant complications, of whom eight (57%) became deaf and six (43%) acquired mixed hearing loss, concluding that the hearing sequela of labyrinthitis was significant; the Taxak and Ram 2020 case report and literature review describes labyrinthitis as inflammation of the inner ear that disrupts transmission of sensory information from the ear to the brain and defines labyrinthitis ossificans as pathological ossification of the membranous labyrinthine spaces in response to an inner-ear insult, presenting with progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; the literature documents hearing loss as the principal residual sequela of labyrinthitis without establishing that the infection caused an individual's hearing loss.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: The mapping does not assert that the labyrinthitis caused an individual's hearing loss: no population cohort quantifies hearing outcome after a defined labyrinthitis episode, the located series is an inpatient complication-rich referral group of fourteen patients in which 57% became deaf, mixed rather than purely sensorineural loss occurred in 43% because of coexisting middle-ear disease, vestibular symptoms are part of the acute presentation rather than a separate outcome, and sudden sensorineural hearing loss has several independent causes (vascular, viral, autoimmune, and retrocochlear disease including vestibular schwannoma) that can produce identical audiometric findings - so no directional claim is made.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized suppurative-inner-ear route is documented: bacterial infection spreading from the middle ear through the round window or the labyrinthine fistula enters the membranous labyrinth, producing purulent labyrinthitis with hair-cell and spiral-ganglion damage; in the healing phase fibroblastic proliferation and subsequent ossification of the labyrinthine spaces (labyrinthitis ossificans) obliterate the cochlear duct, so hearing loss becomes permanent and may progress to profound deafness; the located cohort records this end point as deafness in 57% and mixed hearing loss in 43% of patients, with the individual degree depending on the route of spread, the organism, the timeliness of treatment, and pre-existing middle-ear disease.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Hearing loss is documented as the principal residual sequela of labyrinthitis in a 26-year retrospective cohort and in a case report with literature review, but individual determination requires documentation of the labyrinthitis episode with aetiology and dates, audiometry and imaging localizing the loss to the inner ear, and exclusion of independent causes of hearing loss, with review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Otologic and audiologic documentation of the labyrinthitis episode(s) with aetiology where available (suppurative, cholesteatomatous, viral, or other), laterality, presenting symptoms including vertigo, nystagmus, and hearing change, and treatment with dates; pure-tone audiometry and speech testing establishing the type and degree of hearing loss (sensorineural, mixed, or conductive) with serial measurements and chronology; imaging of the inner ear (high-resolution computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) documenting labyrinthine enhancement, fistula, or ossification; documentation of coexisting middle-ear disease (acute suppurative otitis media, cholesteatomatous chronic otitis media, or chronic otitis media without cholesteatoma) and of any mastoiditis, meningitis, facial paralysis, or intracranial complication; vestibular assessment where relevant, distinguishing peripheral vestibular findings from other causes of dizziness; exclusion of independent causes of sensorineural hearing loss, including noise exposure, ototoxic medication, Meniere's disease, autoimmune inner-ear disease, vascular events, genetic causes, and retrocochlear pathology such as vestibular schwannoma; otolaryngologic or audiologic assessment of whether the labyrinthitis episode materially contributed to the documented hearing loss
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Noise-induced or age-related sensorineural hearing loss
Ototoxic medication exposure (aminoglycosides, platinum chemotherapy, loop diuretics, salicylates)
Meniere's disease or other endolymphatic hydrops
Vascular or thromboembolic sudden sensorineural hearing loss
Retrocochlear pathology (vestibular schwannoma or other cerebellopontine-angle lesion)
Autoimmune inner-ear disease, genetic hearing loss, or otosclerosis
Conductive loss from middle-ear effusion, tympanic-membrane perforation, or ossicular disease alone

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a 26-year retrospective cohort of 14 patients with middle-ear-infection-associated labyrinthitis found that 57% became deaf and 43% acquired mixed hearing loss with the authors concluding the hearing sequela was significant, and a case report with literature review defines the ossificans pathway as pathological ossification of the labyrinthine spaces presenting with progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Because the cohort is small, inpatient, complication-rich, and mixed in audiometric character, and because sudden sensorineural hearing loss has multiple independent causes, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only; the FINAL-CLOSED vestibular-disorder proposition is not reasserted and no vestibular or tinnitus window is authored.

sourceReferences.citation: Maranhao AS, Godofredo VR, Penido Nde O. Suppurative labyrinthitis associated with otitis media: 26 years' experience. Braz J Otorhinolaryngol. 2016 Jan-Feb;82(1):82-7. doi:10.1016/j.bjorl.2014.12.012. PMID 26718959.
sourceReferences.note: Retrospective cohort of 14 patients admitted over 26 years with middle-ear-infection-associated labyrinthitis: eight (57%) became deaf and six (43%) acquired mixed hearing loss, with 24 concomitant complications (labyrinthine fistula six, meningitis five, facial paralysis five, mastoiditis five, cerebellar abscess two, temporal abscess one) and one death - the quantified hearing-sequela anchor.
